events.title: Fortran 90 standardized
events.summary: In July 1991, the Fortran 90 standard was published — the first major modernization of Fortran since 1977, with reusable code modules and whole-array math.
events.about: Fortran 90 let scientists write `A = B + C` on entire arrays instead of hand-written loops, and organize code into reusable modules. It kept Fortran dominant on supercomputers while borrowing ideas from newer languages. Modern Fortran (2003, 2008, 2018) builds on this foundation.

narrative.whyChosen: Fortran 90 was the first big rewrite in fourteen years — array-style math and modules changed how large scientific programs were organized.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept Fortran the default on supercomputers while making code shorter and easier to share across research teams.
narrative.problemSolved: FORTRAN 77 couldn't express modern numerical algorithms cleanly; researchers needed array-level operations and reusable libraries.

events.title: SGI Indigo released
events.summary: Silicon Graphics began shipping the Indigo workstation in July 1991 — an entry-level 3D graphics machine for technical and creative professionals.
events.about: The Indigo ran IRIX Unix with OpenGL-accelerated 3D — game studios, film VFX houses, and CAD firms used it for modeling and rendering. OpenGL itself came from SGI's GL. Developers learning real-time 3D graphics in the 1990s often started on Indigo and Indy workstations before consumer GPUs caught up.

narrative.whyChosen: The Indigo brought SGI's 3D graphics expertise to a wider professional market.
narrative.whyImportant: It helped establish OpenGL and Unix workstations as the standard for 3D content creation.
narrative.problemSolved: Creative studios needed affordable 3D acceleration without mainframe-class price tags.
